summary: Indian Oil buys crude oil, refines it into petrol, diesel, cooking gas and aviation fuel, moves it through its own pipelines, and sells it through petrol pumps, gas agencies and airport fuelling stations.
description: Crude oil is the thick raw liquid pumped from underground. A refinery is a plant that heats it and separates it into fuels and other products. Indian Oil runs refineries, moves the output through long underground pipes, and sells it to drivers at petrol pumps, to homes as cooking gas (LPG, liquefied petroleum gas) in cylinders, to airlines as aircraft fuel, and to factories. It also makes plastics from refinery by-products and sells natural gas.
money: Indian Oil earns money by selling fuels and gas for more than its crude oil, refining, transport and sales costs. Diesel, petrol and cooking gas make up most of what it sells. The gap between what it pays for crude oil and what it charges for products moves from year to year. A customer’s payment is revenue, not profit, and the price of cooking gas for homes is held low, so Indian Oil can lose money on it unless the government pays it back.
customers: Several kinds of customer pay. Drivers pay at petrol pumps, many of them run by dealers (the report lists retail-outlet dealers) who buy fuel from Indian Oil. Households pay for LPG cylinders through gas distributors. Airlines pay for aircraft fuel. Factories, road builders and other businesses buy fuel, bitumen (the black material used to surface roads) and plastic raw material in bulk. For household cooking gas, the government also pays Indian Oil part of the cost when the selling price is set below cost.
drivers: The price of crude oil compared with the price of the fuel it sells, how much of its refining capacity runs, and whether the government lets prices cover costs, including cooking gas for homes.

groups.title: Petrol and diesel pumps
groups.examples: A car filling up at an Indian Oil pump, or a lorry buying diesel on a highway.
groups.explanation: Indian Oil sells petrol and diesel through a network of retail outlets, which are petrol pumps, many run by dealers. The report counts 42,818 outlets, and some also offer rest stops and electric charging.

groups.title: Cooking gas (Indane)
groups.examples: A red cylinder delivered to a kitchen, or piped gas to a home.
groups.explanation: Indian Oil sells LPG cylinders under the Indane brand through gas distributors who deliver to homes. It also sells LPG to businesses. Its report puts its share of the household LPG market at about 46%.

groups.title: Aviation fuel, bitumen and lubricants
groups.examples: Fuel for an aeroplane, the black surface of a new road, or engine oil sold under the Servo brand.
groups.explanation: Indian Oil fills aircraft at airport fuelling stations, sells bitumen to road builders and sells lubricants, which are oils that keep engines and machines moving smoothly.

groups.title: Petrochemicals
groups.examples: Plastic granules for packaging, raw material for polyester cloth.
groups.explanation: Petrochemicals are plastics and chemicals made from refinery by-products. Indian Oil says this lets it earn more from what comes out of its refineries, instead of selling only fuel.

groups.title: Natural gas and electric charging
groups.examples: CNG (compressed natural gas) for vehicles, gas to homes through city networks, and charging or battery swapping for electric vehicles.
groups.explanation: Indian Oil, with its joint ventures (businesses it owns together with partners), holds permission to supply city gas in 49 areas. It also runs CNG stations and electric vehicle charging and battery-swapping points.

groups.title: Refineries and pipelines
groups.examples: A refinery with tall towers, and pipes that run for hundreds of kilometres underground.
groups.explanation: These are the plants and pipes behind the other products. They are not sold to customers directly, but they make the fuel and carry crude oil and fuel in bulk to where it is needed.

basics.title: What is a refinery, and what comes out of it?
basics.text: A refinery heats crude oil and separates it into parts that boil at different temperatures. These become petrol, diesel, aviation fuel, LPG, bitumen and raw material for plastics. Indian Oil’s report counts 10 refineries in its group, including one owned by a listed subsidiary, Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL).

basics.title: What is an oil marketing company?
basics.text: An oil marketing company (OMC) sells fuel to the public. Indian Oil is both a refiner and an OMC, so it makes fuel and sells it. The report calls the money between buying crude oil and selling products the refining margin and the marketing margin.

basics.title: Why does the government matter for cooking gas?
basics.text: The government wants household LPG to stay affordable. When the price charged to homes is below the market price, Indian Oil carries the shortfall. The report says the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas approved compensation to Indian Oil for this, paid in 12 equal monthly instalments starting November 2025.

steps.title: Buy crude oil
steps.text: Indian Oil buys crude oil from different suppliers and brings it to its refineries. Its report says it has widened its crude buying to several sources, to cut the risk of one supply route being cut off.

steps.title: Refine it into products
steps.text: The refineries turn crude oil into petrol, diesel, LPG, aircraft fuel, bitumen and plastics raw material. Running them close to full capacity spreads their fixed costs over more product.

steps.title: Move it in bulk
steps.text: Pipelines carry crude oil and finished fuel over long distances, which is usually cheaper than trucks. The report counts 20,009 km of pipelines. Trucks, rail and ships do the rest of the delivery.

steps.title: Sell through outlets, agencies and big customers
steps.text: Fuel reaches drivers through dealers’ petrol pumps, homes through gas distributors, and airlines and factories directly. Typically, dealers and distributors buy from the company and keep a margin on what they sell.

steps.title: Get paid, and claim the shortfall on cooking gas
steps.text: Revenue (what Indian Oil bills), profit (what is left after costs) and cash in hand are three different things. For household LPG sold below cost, the company waits for the government’s compensation before that part counts as revenue.

specifics.title: Household cooking gas can be sold below cost
specifics.text: The retail price of domestic LPG is not set freely. The report states that where this price is below the market price, the company kept the difference in a separate buffer account and did not count that part as revenue. Government compensation then reduces the buffer.

specifics.title: Refining and selling are two margins
specifics.text: Indian Oil earns a refining margin (crude oil to products) and a marketing margin (products to customers). The report says its operating profit improved on better refining and marketing margins, helped by cheaper crude oil. It also notes years with suppressed marketing margins.

specifics.title: One group, several companies
specifics.text: Chennai Petroleum Corporation Limited (CPCL) is a separately listed subsidiary, and several gas, LNG (liquefied natural gas, gas cooled into a liquid for shipping) and battery-swapping businesses are joint ventures. Which of these sit inside a reported number depends on whether it is standalone or consolidated.

specifics.title: Turnover is mostly diesel and petrol
specifics.text: On a standalone basis (Indian Oil alone), the company’s sustainability report lists high-speed diesel at 44.75% of turnover and motor spirit (petrol) at 23.28%. LPG is 11.63% and aviation fuel 4.37%.

watch: How much of the cooking-gas shortfall is repaid, and how fast?
The report shows compensation arrives in monthly instalments, so a late or smaller payment would leave a gap in revenue.
Read the note on domestic LPG revenue in the latest annual report, and check whether the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has issued new compensation letters since October 2025.
How wide are the refining and marketing margins?
The report links the swing in operating profit to these two margins and to the cost of crude oil.
In each quarterly results release, compare the refining margin and the marketing margin with the same quarter a year earlier, and note what the company says changed the crude oil cost.
Where does the crude oil come from, and what happens if a route closes?
The report names Middle East tensions and the Strait of Hormuz as a supply risk and says it widened its crude sourcing.
Read the risk management section and the crude buying discussion each year, and compare the list of supply sources and routes to see whether it is becoming wider or narrower.
How quickly are electric vehicles, biofuels and hydrogen replacing petrol and diesel?
The report lists changing fuel demand as a competitive risk, and the company is investing in these fields.
Read the new-energy section of the annual report, then compare petrol, diesel and LPG sales volumes with electric charging, battery swapping and biofuel sales from year to year.
How much does the group depend on subsidiaries and joint ventures?
Standalone and consolidated numbers differ, and the refinery count includes CPCL.
Compare the standalone and consolidated statements in the annual report, and read the list of subsidiaries and joint ventures to see which businesses sit inside each reported number.
risks: Plant outages and fuel supply constraints
The report lists possible plant outages and feedstock (raw material) shortages. A refinery that stops still has to pay its costs, and customers may buy elsewhere.
The report says tensions in the Middle East and around the Strait of Hormuz, a key sea route for crude oil and gas, can disrupt supply and push up freight and insurance costs.
Large building projects need long-term money
Capacity expansions at several refineries need funding over many years. The report lists these capital programmes among its financial risks.
Competition across new and old energy segments
The report lists more competition in both conventional fuels and newer energy segments, which can pull customers or margins away.
context: Government compensation for household cooking gas

The report says the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas approved compensation by letters of 3 and 24 October 2025 for losses on domestic LPG sold below cost. It is paid in 12 equal monthly instalments, counted month by month from November 2025.
sources: Indian Oil Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report 2025-26

stepsTitle: From crude oil to a full tank.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: Indian Oil refines crude oil into petrol, diesel, cooking gas, aircraft fuel and plastics raw material, carries it through pipelines, and sells it through petrol pumps and gas agencies.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Drivers, households, airlines and factories pay for fuel and gas. For household cooking gas the government also pays part of the cost back to the company.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: It sells fuels and gas for more than its costs of buying crude oil, refining, moving and selling. Petrol, diesel and cooking gas bring in most of its sales.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Crude oil and imported gas are the biggest cost, then running refineries and pipelines, delivery, and building new plants.

helps.title: Crude oil to petrol pump in one group
helps.text: The report describes an integrated chain of refining, pipelines and marketing, and says land, pipeline rights-of-way and outlet permissions make it hard for a new entrant to copy.

helps.title: Plastics add a second use for refinery output
helps.text: The report says petrochemicals raise the value from refinery streams and extend the business beyond transport fuels, into packaging, textiles and plastics.

helps.title: Refineries that handle many types of crude
helps.text: The report says a wider mix of crude oil reduces concentration risk and gives more choice in what to buy as conditions change.

hurts.title: Crude oil and freight prices swing
hurts.text: The report lists crude oil price swings, freight costs and inflation as risks to buying costs, refining margins and the cash tied up in stock.

hurts.title: Exchange rates raise import costs
hurts.text: Crude oil is bought in foreign currency, so a weaker rupee makes imports dearer. The report lists exchange rate changes as a financial risk.

hurts.title: Demand patterns are changing
hurts.text: The report lists rising use of electric vehicles, hydrogen and biofuels and changing fuel demand as a risk to fuel sales over time.
